title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Scripture elect Resp close: Accepted-in-the-Beloved and Eph 2 show justification begins at faith
pass_a_gloss: Nor does that stand in the way, He had us accepted in his beloved Son: For the Greek verb ἐχαρίτωσεν seems rather to be referred to the present state of the elect already regenerated than to God’s eternal purpose. Whence Beza translates, He freely makes them gracious to himself, namely He has now freely justified and admitted the believers themselves into the state of actual reconciliation; But if someone interprets that acceptance of God’s eternal love by which he embraces the elect not yet born, that acceptance will denote the purpose of communicating his goodness, not the act itself of communication, as was answered above from Aquinas. Beza also in his Commentaries on verse 5 rightly observed that the elect in their own time obtain wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption freely through faith: therefore they were not from eternity justified, sanctified, or reconciled, although elect and predestined from eternity. But no one taught this more clearly than the Apostle himself, who demonstrates that those very ones whom he called elect before the foundations of the world were laid were nevertheless by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3), and long remained without Christ, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, without God in the world: Then truly in Christ Jesus those who once were far off were made near, when through the blood of Christ apprehended by faith they were reconciled to God (Ephesians 2:12, 13, and following). If therefore we give faith to Paul, although the election and predestination of humans is eternal from God’s eternal love, yet their justification and reconciliation is not to be said to be manifested or revealed when they believe in Christ, but then first to come to be and to be constituted.
pass_b_english: Nor does the clause “he had us accepted in his beloved Son” block this (Ephesians 1:6). The Greek verb ἐχαρίτωσεν seems to point to the present state of the elect already regenerated, more than to God’s eternal purpose. So Beza renders it, “he freely makes them gracious to himself”—that is, he has now freely justified believers and admitted them into the state of actual reconciliation. If someone reads that acceptance as God’s eternal love embracing the elect not yet born, then the acceptance names the purpose of communicating his goodness, not the act of communication itself—as was already answered from Aquinas above. Beza also notes rightly in his comments on verse 5 that the elect obtain wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption freely through faith in their own time. They were not, then, justified, sanctified, or reconciled from eternity, though they were elect and predestined from eternity (Ephesians 1:5). No one taught this more clearly than the Apostle himself. The very people he called elect before the world’s foundations were laid he also shows were by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3), and long remained without Christ, aliens from Israel’s commonwealth, strangers to the covenants of promise, without hope, and without God in the world. Then, in Christ Jesus, those who were once far off were made near when, through Christ’s blood grasped by faith, they were reconciled to God (Ephesians 2:12–13 and following). If we trust Paul, then—however eternal human election and predestination are from God’s eternal love—their justification and reconciliation are not to be called a mere manifestation or unveiling when they believe in Christ. That is when they first come to be and are constituted.
source_text: Neque obstat illud, Acceptos nos habuit in dilecto suo Filio: Nam Graecum verbum ἐχαρίτωσεν potius ad praesentem statum electorum jam regeneratorum quam ad aeternum Dei propositum referri videtur. Unde Beza vertit, gratis efficit sibi gratos, nempe gratis nunc justificavit & in statum actualis reconciliationis admisit ipsos credentes; Quod si quis illam acceptationem de aeterno Dei amore interpretetur, quo electos nondum natos complectitur, acceptatio illa propositum communicandi bonitatem suam, non ipsum actum communicationis denotabit, ut ex Aquinate supra responsum est. Beza etiam in Commentariis suis ad vers. 5. recte observavit Electos suo tempore sapientiam, justitiam, sanctificationem, redemptionem gratis per fidem adipisci: non igitur ab aeterno justificati sanctificati aut reconciliati, quamvis electi & praedestinati ab aeterno. Sed nemo clarius hoc docuit quam ipse Apostolus, qui eos ipsos, quos dixit electos ante jacta mundi fundamenta, tamen natura fuisse filios irae demonstrat, Ephes. ii. 3. & ac diu mansisse absque Christo, alienos a Republica Israelis, & extraneos a pactis promissionis, spem non habentes, Deo expertes in mundo: Tunc vero in Christo Jesu qui olim erant procul propinquos factos fuisse, cum per sanguinem Christi fide apprehensi Deo reconciliati essent, vers. 12, 13, &c. Si igitur Paulo fidem adhibemus, utcunque electio & praedestinatio hominum sit ab aeterno Dei amore aeterna, tamen justificatio & reconciliatio eorundem non manifestari aut revelari dicenda est quando credunt in Christum, sed tum primum fieri & constitui.
